name: Esther Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Most days I'm on campus for two or three classes, English literature and a history seminar on the industrial revolution, which I love. Three evenings a week I work the counter at the cinema café, making hot chocolates and mopping up popcorn. I share a flat with two girls from my course, and we split the heating bill very carefully.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's been harder than you expected?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money, honestly. I thought a loan would cover everything and it covers the fees and about half the rent. The café pays by the hour, so if a film flops and they send us home early, I feel it in my food shop that week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. That one is called AI Plateau. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful in a small way and overhyped everywhere else. I use it now and then to tidy up a reading list or explain a hard poem, but I wouldn't let it write for me. Mostly I'd say we should stay calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm worried about money rather than AI. The loan is big, and the cinema café could cut hours any week if audiences drop. An English degree isn't a straight path to a job, and I'm not sure what I'll do after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on. I'd keep my three evening shifts, ask for a fourth in the summer and go to the careers talks for English students. I'd also try writing for the student newspaper, because journalists get hired on what they've published.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, a bit tired, a bit hopeful. If life stays like this I can manage it, but only just.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a week when the café sends you home early?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lose around thirty pounds, which sounds small but it's my food budget. Last month I ate pasta with nothing on it three nights running. My flatmate noticed and quietly made too much curry, which was kind but a bit humiliating.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the student newspaper rather than something safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like it and because nobody gives you a chance to write unless you show up. It's unpaid and I'm already tired. But I'd rather try and be a bit poorer than not try at all.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but overhyped**, and people should stay calm.
I'd say my generation needs **proper careers advice**.
think: I'm more worried about **rent and hours** at the café than about AI.
An English degree isn't a straight path, and I don't know my **next step**.
do: Keep three **café shifts** and ask for a fourth in the summer.
Start writing for the **student newspaper** to build a portfolio.
feel: A bit tired and a bit hopeful, **managing but only just**.
S0.quote: I lose around thirty pounds, which sounds small but it's my food budget. Last month I ate pasta with nothing on it three nights running.
fieldNote: Esther's mood is driven by **hours and rent**, not AI.
Uses AI lightly, and has a clear line about not letting it write for her.
Embarrassed by receiving charity from a flatmate.

steps.text: Keep three evening shifts at the cinema café
Ask for a fourth shift over the summer
Put ten pounds a week into a savings pot

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. That one is called Steady Disruption. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it will change who gets hired, and we need public support for people who get left behind. Governments have let universities and services run short of money for years, and now they'll say we need to adapt. I'd say that online and probably in my seminar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing is my whole degree, and writing is the first thing the card says AI takes. A lot of entry-level jobs for English graduates are marketing copy, proofreading and press office work. I'd think the jobs I'd apply for in 2029 may have shrunk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get better at using AI properly, as a research and editing helper, and learn what it gets wrong, because employers will want that. I'd try for a placement with a local paper or a museum in second year. I'd also look at a teaching route as a backup, since schools still need people in a room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit scared, but there's some excitement mixed in. I don't want to be the person who ignored it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you decide when to rely on AI and when not to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it for the dull parts, like summarising or checking my grammar. I wouldn't use it for ideas or opinions, because that's what I'm being taught to do. If a tool can write my essays, my degree isn't worth much, so I'd rather get good at the part it can't do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is responsible for helping people like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, mostly, because it sets the funding. Then employers, who should still hire and train juniors instead of using software. I don't think students should have to fix this alone, but I know we'll be the ones who have to adapt first.

say: I'd say the government should **fund support** for people who get left behind.
I'd say employers must keep **training juniors**.
think: Writing is my whole degree, so **entry-level jobs** I want may shrink.
I'd be afraid of being the one who **ignored it**.
do: Learn to use AI as a **research and editing helper** and check its mistakes.
Look for a **museum or local paper** placement and keep teaching as a backup.
feel: A bit **scared**, with some excitement mixed in.
S1.quote: If a tool can write my essays, my degree isn't worth much, so I'd rather get good at the part it can't do.
fieldNote: She treats AI as a **tool with limits**, which suits her steady adaptability.
Blames governments for funding more than firms.
Teaching is her fallback, a human-contact job she trusts.

steps.text: Use AI to summarise reading and check my own drafts
Apply for a museum or local paper placement
Sign the students' petition on graduate support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. That one is called AGI by 2028. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's terrifying and the government has done nothing to prepare. Two years isn't enough to change schools, jobs or benefits. I'd be saying that to anyone who'd listen, and probably writing about it for the student paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think my degree might not matter by the time I graduate. If AI does almost any thinking job by 2028, then writing, marketing and teaching assistants are all in trouble. I'd be thinking about whether to stay at university or find something that still exists.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd talk to the careers service the next week and my personal tutor. I'd probably keep going at university because the loan is already taken, but I'd work more shifts and save every pound I could. I'd also ask my parents what the family could do together, like moving back in if it got really bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. I'd feel like my plans were taken from me before I'd had a chance to try them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years, what would you do differently from a longer warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop planning the long way round. No postgraduate study, no unpaid internships. I'd go straight to anything stable, probably a hands-on job in health or care, which the card says survive about three years longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm sorry, I know you worked hard for me to get here. I'd ask if I could come home if I need to, and I'd offer to pay a bit of rent from my café wages. I'd hate asking, but I'd rather ask than hide it.

say: I'd say **two years** isn't enough to prepare schools, jobs or benefits.
I'd write about it in the **student newspaper**.
think: My degree might **not matter** by the time I graduate.
I'd wonder whether to stay at university or find something that **still exists**.
do: See the **careers service** and my tutor within the week.
Work **extra shifts** and save, and ask my parents about moving home.
feel: **Heavy**, as if my plans were taken before I could try them.
S2.quote: I'd feel like my plans were taken from me before I'd had a chance to try them.
fieldNote: Becomes **practical and defensive** under the short warning.
Considers moving home, which she dislikes but names honestly.
Looks to health and care jobs as the hands-on fallback.

steps.text: Book a careers service appointment within the week
Look for hands-on work in health or care
Cut my food shop to a strict weekly budget
Pick up extra shifts and save every spare pound

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. That one is called AGI by 2031. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives us a real chance if the government and universities act now. I'd want them to rewrite courses and promise graduate jobs, not wait until the day it lands. I'd bring it up at student meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I think I'd get my degree before it fully lands, but I'd be job hunting in the first years of it. That's the hardest time to be a graduate. I might use the time to learn something that holds its value, maybe teaching or a skill with people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish English and history, and in second year start a teaching conversion or look at journalism placements. I'd get comfortable with AI tools now, so that I'm not behind. I'd save a bit each month from the café, and ask for a pay rise when I'm third-year senior.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but not hopeless. There's enough time to try two or three things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you try first in the first year of seeing it coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to a school to volunteer for a few weeks and see if teaching suits me. I'd also start a proper portfolio, with real articles under my name. If one of those works, great, and if not I'll know early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is five years different from two or ten?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two is panic, ten is easy to ignore. Five is the sort of time where you can't pretend and still have enough room to move. That's the stage I'd work hardest.

say: I'd say five years is a **real chance** if schools and universities change courses now.
I'd push for **graduate job guarantees** in student meetings.
think: I'd be job hunting in the **first years** of AGI, the hardest time for graduates.
I might aim for something with **people contact**, like teaching.
do: Volunteer in a **school** to see if teaching suits me.
Build a **portfolio** of real articles and get used to AI tools.
feel: **Nervous**, but not hopeless, because there is room to try things.
S3.quote: Two is panic, ten is easy to ignore. Five is the sort of time where you can't pretend and still have enough room to move.
fieldNote: Describes the **three timelines** in her own terms, which shows clear thinking.
Treats time as a window to test options rather than panic.
Still unsure which route will actually pay.

steps.text: Volunteer in a local school for a few weeks
Practise AI tools on my essays and research
Save fifteen pounds a week from café wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. That one is called AGI by 2036. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough if we use it, and I'd want the government to start training programmes now. People shouldn't treat it like science fiction. I'd say it online, and I'd say it to my dad, who thinks it's all hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel okay about my own life. I'd have a degree, maybe a teaching qualification, and years of savings. The thing I'd worry about is my younger cousins and the future of work for them, since they'll arrive in the job market just as it lands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, and then train as a teacher or find a communications job, whichever opens. I'd pay off part of the loan early and start a small pension. I'd also keep learning new tools every year so that I'm never far behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, with a little curiosity. Ten years is like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your dad that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, Dad, you don't have to take my word for it, but please talk to someone who knows. He runs a small repair shop and he'd think it's about him. I'd tell him there's time and we could plan it together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the government to do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fund training and make sure it's open to people who can't afford it. I'd rather the money goes to schools and hospitals, because those are the jobs people trust.

say: I'd say ten years is enough if **training starts now**.
I'd tell my dad it isn't science fiction and we can **plan together**.
think: My own life looks **okay**, with a degree and a few years of savings.
I worry more about my **younger cousins** arriving just as it lands.
do: Finish my degree and train as a **teacher** or find a communications job.
Pay down part of the **loan early** and keep learning new tools each year.
feel: **Calm**, with some curiosity, because ten years feels like a long runway.
S4.quote: I'd rather the money goes to schools and hospitals, because those are the jobs people trust.
fieldNote: Her **calm** comes from time, and she switches to worrying about family.
Brings her father into the answer, showing a warm family tie.
Policy views stay consistent: fund public services and training.

steps.text: Complete the degree and apply for teacher training
Pay part of the student loan early
Learn one new AI tool every year
Vote for parties that fund schools and hospitals

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. It leaves no time for anything, not for schools, not for families, not for me. What would help is a government that actually funds retraining, a careers service that gives honest advice, and employers who keep hiring juniors.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that students are often treated like we're all fine. Many of us are managing on thirty pounds a week and a cinema café wage. If someone wants to know what AI means for us, start by asking how we're paying for lunch.

headlineQuote: If someone wants to know what AI means for us, start by asking how we're paying for lunch.
portrait: Esther, 18, studies **English and history** and works evenings at a cinema café while sharing a flat.
She uses AI now and then but wants to keep her own **ideas and voice**.
She blames **government underfunding** more than firms and wants public support and training.
Thin money makes even quiet scenarios feel anxious, and the two-year picture alarms her.
She plans around journalism or teaching, and she would move home if she had to.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most, because it leaves no time for families, schools or students.
whatWouldHelp: Government-funded **retraining**, honest careers advice and employers who keep hiring juniors.
